In settings where more intensive strategies may be required, it is suggested that these strategies should be periodically re-evaluated to determine whether further intensification is necessary. 2. Current evidence does not establish an optimal prevalence threshold for discontinuing preventive chemotherapy programs. 3. There is insufficient data to support a test-and-treat strategy except in scenarios where preventive chemotherapy is not recommended. This is partly due to the higher resource demands of such strategies and the need for highly sensitive diagnostic tests. 4. Historically, the World Health Organization (WHO) has recommended the use of praziquantel at a dose of 40–60 mg/kg as a single annual dose for preventive chemotherapy programs. 5. This dosing regimen was based on a randomized trial that demonstrated equivalent outcomes between 40 mg/kg and 60 mg/kg doses. 6. A larger body of research has explored two-dose regimens and varying dosing strategies, which may improve efficacy in certain contexts. However, current evidence supports single-dose administration as a balance between efficacy and operational feasibility. 7. The dose of praziquantel is now determined using a dose pole, which estimates a person’s weight based on their height and provides a color-coded guide for the number of pills required to achieve the recommended dose per kilogram. 8. Preventive chemotherapy has been a cornerstone of the success of most programs that have eliminated schistosomiasis as a public health problem and are now working towards interrupting transmission or awaiting verification of this achievement. 9. In countries that have achieved success, the core elements of control and elimination strategies have included combinations of: (i) reducing adult worms and eggs through preventive chemotherapy, (ii) eliminating intermediate snail hosts, (iii) reducing water contamination, and (iv) preventing human infection through sanitation and hygiene measures. 10. Most programs have incorporated some degree of community education and engagement, which has been critical to their success. 11. Sustained political will and determination to achieve elimination goals have been key factors in the success of these programs, even after severe morbidity from infection has been controlled. 12. When severe morbidity is controlled through sustained preventive chemotherapy programs, there is a risk that countries may shift their focus and resources to other public health issues, potentially leading to a resurgence in transmission, infection, and disease within the community. This underscores the importance of continuing efforts towards the elimination of schistosomiasis transmission. 13. Evidence from countries awaiting verification of transmission interruption indicates that preventive chemotherapy has been a major contributor to their success. 14. WHO recommends that preventive chemotherapy remains a key component of programs that have reduced prevalence to below 10%. This should be reinforced by ensuring the availability of praziquantel in health centers for infected individuals of all ages. 15. Programs must maintain flexibility to account for regional and local variations as they progress towards elimination. 16. In communities with baseline Schistosoma prevalence below 10% and no prior history of mass drug administration (MDA) with praziquantel, preventive chemotherapy can be administered less frequently, such as once every 2–3 years. This aims to reduce endemicity, prevent a rebound in infection prevalence, and sustain efforts towards transmission interruption. 17. Clinical studies support the availability of praziquantel treatment for infected individuals in a test-and-treat strategy, including for preschool-aged children. 18. The Guideline Development Group (GDG) reached a consensus on recommending a threshold of 10% parasitological prevalence (measured by Kato-Katz or urine filtration) for initiating preventive chemotherapy. 19. A systematic review assessed the effects of varying frequencies of preventive chemotherapy with praziquantel on Schistosoma infections in at-risk populations. It included randomized and quasi-randomized trials comparing biannual and annual treatment regimens. 20. The review identified three cluster-randomized controlled trials that met inclusion criteria, focusing on parasitological outcomes such as prevalence and infection intensity in at-risk populations, including school-aged children, older adolescents, and adults. 21. The first trial, conducted in Senegal, compared annual and biannual school-based preventive chemotherapy with praziquantel in villages endemic for Schistosoma haematobium and Schistosoma mansoni. The main outcomes were prevalence and infection intensity after one year. 22. The second trial, conducted in Niger, involved 22,372 participants from 225 villages endemic for Schistosoma haematobium. Villages were randomized to receive annual or biannual school-based or community-wide treatment, with outcomes measured over five years. 23. The third trial, conducted in a smaller cohort of 377 primary school children in Kenya, compared single-dose praziquantel treatment at baseline versus treatment at baseline and six months. 24. The evidence suggests that biannual treatment may provide greater benefits in settings with higher baseline prevalence, particularly for Schistosoma haematobium. However, data for Schistosoma mansoni and other species are limited and of lower quality. 25. Modeling studies indicate that increasing the frequency of preventive chemotherapy from annual to biannual treatment can significantly reduce infection prevalence and intensity, particularly in high-prevalence settings. This approach is also highly cost-effective. 26. Persistent hot spots, defined as communities with high prevalence despite repeated preventive chemotherapy, may benefit from biannual treatment. However, these communities are challenging to identify based on baseline prevalence alone. 27. The GDG determined that a relative reduction in prevalence of less than 30% after two years of annual preventive chemotherapy with ≥75% treatment coverage suggests a hot spot community that may require more intensive intervention. 28. The choice of criteria for identifying hot spots and determining the need for biannual treatment may vary based on baseline prevalence and epidemiological context.
